entry: Indian [[Curry|curry]] dish of chicken in a rich, creamy tomato and butter gravy. Also called murgh makhani, it was popularized in the 1950s at the Moti Mahal restaurant in Daryaganj, [[Delhi]], where it is often said to have been invented. Its origin is disputed: some accounts place its creation in [[Peshawar]] before the [[Partition of India|partition of India]], and a 2024 lawsuit between the Gujral and Jaggi families, who run rival restaurants, contests credit for the invention.

Country in [[Mainland Southeast Asia]] (pop., 2024: 17.6 million). Officially the Kingdom of Cambodia, it borders Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam and has a coastline on the [[Gulf of Thailand]]. In AD 802 [[Jayavarman II]] declared himself king, and the [[Khmer Empire]] that followed spread [[Hinduism]] and later Buddhism across the region. In 1863 the country became a French protectorate, and it gained independence in 1953. The [[Khmer Rouge]] regime carried out the [[Cambodian genocide]] from 1975 to 1979, until a Vietnamese intervention ousted it. By 1993, a [[United Nations]] peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and a democratic constitution. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy in which the Cambodian People's Party dominates politics, and agriculture remains its dominant economic sector.

Systematic persecution and killing of Cambodian citizens by the [[Khmer Rouge]] regime, 1975–79. Led by [[Pol Pot]], the regime emptied the cities and forced people into labor camps, where executions, starvation, and disease were widespread. An estimated 1.5 to 2 million people died, roughly 20 to 25% of the 1975 population. At least 90% of the foreign aid the Khmer Rouge received came from China, whose [[Chinese Communist Party]] was led by [[Mao Zedong]]. A Vietnamese invasion toppled the regime in 1978. In 2003 the government and the [[United Nations]] agreed to establish the Extraordinary Chambers in the Court of Cambodia, which in 2019 sentenced [[Nuon Chea]] and Khieu Samphan to life imprisonment.

Even-toed ungulate in the genus Camelus, marked by fatty deposits on its back. Camels have long been domesticated as [[Livestock|livestock]], providing milk, meat, and fiber, and they serve as working animals suited to desert habitats. Three species survive: the one-humped [[Dromedary|dromedary]], which makes up 94% of the world's camels; the two-humped [[Bactrian camel]]; and the wild Bactrian camel, which is endangered, with about 1,000 individuals. The humps are fat reserves rather than water stores, although dromedaries can drink up to 140 L at a time. Camelids originated in North America during the [[Eocene]], and the ancestor of modern camels crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late [[Miocene]], around 6 million years ago.

Geologic shield, a large area of exposed [[Precambrian]] igneous and metamorphic rock forming the core of [[North America]]. Also called the Laurentian Shield, it forms the [[Craton|North American craton]] and extends across eastern and central [[Canada]], centered on [[Hudson Bay]]. Its exposed area is about 8,000,000 sq km (3,100,000 sq mi), including much of Greenland, most of Quebec, and much of Ontario. Glaciation left only a thin soil layer over the bedrock and produced a dense, irregular pattern of rivers and lakes. Rocks in the region date from 2.5 to 4.2 billion years ago, and many of Canada's major ore deposits are associated with greenstone belts.

Annual film festival held in [[Cannes]], France. Founded in 1946, the invitation-only festival previews new films of all genres, including documentaries, and is usually held in May. Its origins lie in 1938, when [[Benito Mussolini|Mussolini]] and [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] overruled jury decisions at the [[Venice Film Festival]] and jurors from France, Britain, and the United States withdrew. French officials then set up a rival international festival. Postponed by [[World War II]], it was first held from September 20 to October 5, 1946, with films from 21 countries. The Palme d'Or, introduced in 1955, is its top prize. Critics have questioned its selection processes, which some argue favor arthouse films over commercially oriented productions.

Administrative region in northeastern [[Mindanao]], Philippines. Designated Region XIII, it was created by Republic Act No. 7901 on February 23, 1995. The region comprises five provinces and six cities, with [[Butuan]] as its administrative center. Its name is taken from the Kalagan people. Before colonial times, the [[Butuan (historical polity)|Butuan polity]] was a powerful Hindu state known for goldsmithing and boat-making.

Class of iron–carbon alloys with more than 2% carbon and about 1–3% silicon. Its relatively low melting point, good fluidity, and castability make it suitable for pipes, machine parts, and [[Automotive industry|automotive]] components such as cylinder heads and blocks. Cast iron tends to be brittle, and it is notoriously difficult to weld. The form of its carbon determines its properties: white cast iron contains hard but brittle [[Cementite]], while [[Graphite]] flakes in gray cast iron deflect cracks. The earliest cast-iron artifacts date to the 8th century BC and were found in what is now [[Jiangsu]], [[China]]. In ancient China it was used to mass-produce weapons, and in 15th-century [[Burgundy]] it was cast into [[Cannon|cannons]]. The first cast-iron bridge, [[The Iron Bridge]] in Shropshire, England, was built in the 1770s.

Condition of fame and broad public recognition resulting from [[Mass media|mass media]] attention. The word also refers to famous individuals, who may attain celebrity through wealth, sports, entertainment, politics, or a connection to another celebrity. Unlike the neutral terms *famous* or *notable*, it usually implies a favorable public image. Historian Greg Jenner dates the earliest celebrities to the early 1700s, though athletes in [[Ancient Greece]] were welcomed home as heroes, and [[Julius Caesar]] appeared on a coin in his own lifetime. [[Lord Byron]] became a celebrity in 1812 after publishing the first two cantos of *Childe Harold's Pilgrimage*. Expanding mass media has since broadened the ways people become famous.

Prefecture-level city in northwestern [[Hunan]] province, [[China]]. Known as Wuling in antiquity, it lies west of [[Dongting Lake]] and has been called Changde since the 12th century. Its Pengtoushan site contains the earliest evidence of a settled village found in China. The city is known for the Battle of Changde in the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] (1937–45) and for atrocities by the Imperial Japanese Army. Its 3 km Poetry Wall along the Yuan River is listed in the *Guinness Book of World Records* as the longest wall with engraved art.

Fundamental rights and freedoms against government restriction except by due process of law. Their scope varies by country, but they often include freedom of [[Freedom of speech|speech]], [[Freedom of religion|religion]], assembly, and the press, along with the right to privacy, equality before the law, and the right to a fair trial. Many nations enumerate them in a [[Bill of rights|bill of rights]], and the concept is often traced to the [[Magna Carta]] of 1215. Libertarians emphasize negative liberty, or freedom from government intervention, a view associated with [[John Stuart Mill]] and [[Friedrich Hayek]]. Whether some claimed rights, such as property rights, [[Reproductive rights|reproductive rights]], and civil marriage, qualify as civil liberties is disputed, as is their suspension in wartime or during a [[State of emergency|state of emergency]].

City on the southern shore of [[Lake Erie]], [[Ohio]], U.S. (pop., 2020: 372,624). Founded in 1796 by surveyors of the Connecticut Land Company, it was named for General Moses Cleaveland, a veteran of the [[American Revolutionary War]]. Its location on the Cuyahoga River and Lake Erie gave it access to [[Great Lakes]] trade, and it grew rapidly after the Ohio and Erie Canal opened in 1832. Cleveland was among the 10 largest U.S. cities for much of the 20th century. Manufacturing decline and [[Suburb|suburbanization]] slowed its economy from the 1960s. Its economy relies on higher education, healthcare, financial services, and biomedicine, and the city is home to the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Small ground-nesting game bird in the pheasant family [[Phasianidae]]. Mainly migratory, it breeds across the Palearctic and winters in Africa and southern India. It is widespread in Europe and North Africa and is classified as least concern globally. Its characteristic call of three repeated chirps makes it more often heard than seen, since it keeps hidden in crops and prefers to creep away rather than fly. It feeds on seeds and ground-dwelling insects, and like the Japanese quail it is sometimes kept as [[Poultry|poultry]]. Swedish naturalist [[Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in 1758 as *Tetrao coturnix*, and five subspecies are recognized.

Group of mostly evergreen, cone-bearing [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperm]] trees and shrubs. With over 600 living species, conifers are wind-pollinated and bear separate male and female cones. They first appear in the [[Fossil|fossil]] record over 300 million years ago, in the [[Carboniferous]], and became dominant land plants in the [[Mesozoic]]. Conifers dominate the [[Taiga|taiga]] of the Northern Hemisphere, where boreal species have conical shapes that shed snow and waxy, needle-shaped leaves that reduce water loss. The world's tallest living trees are conifers, including the [[Sequoia sempervirens|coast redwood]], which reaches 116.07 m. As of 2025, 94 conifer species are listed as endangered, and conifers are of great economic value for timber and paper.

Compulsory enlistment into national or military service, enforced by law. The modern system of near-universal conscription for young men dates to the [[French Revolution]] in the 1790s, although the practice is much older. The Babylonian Empire under [[Hammurabi]] (1791–1750 BC) required military service in wartime and labor in peacetime under a system called *ilkum*. Objections include conscientious and political opposition, and the fact that the draft has usually applied only to men. Some states offer alternative civil service, such as *Zivildienst* in [[Austria]] and Switzerland. Many states have abolished conscription, though many keep the power to resume it in wartime. The [[United Kingdom]] abolished conscription in 1960, and it has not been enforced in the [[United States]] since 1973.

Bond convertible by the holder into a specified number of shares of the issuer's common stock. It is a [[Hybrid security|hybrid security]] with debt and equity features, and its yield is typically lower than that of similar nonconvertible debt. The issuer benefits from reduced interest payments, but conversion dilutes existing shareholders. Convertible notes are also a common vehicle for seed investing in startups. The instrument dates to the mid-19th century, when speculators such as Jacob Little and Daniel Drew used it to counter market cornering.

Choice and willingness to confront agony, pain, danger, uncertainty, or intimidation. Physical courage is bravery in the face of pain, hardship, or death, while moral courage is the ability to act rightly despite popular opposition, shame, or scandal. The classical virtue of fortitude, which includes perseverance and patience, is also translated as courage. Western philosophers including [[Socrates]], [[Plato]], and [[Aristotle]] wrote on the subject, and the [[Tao Te Ching]] offers extensive thoughts on courage in the Eastern tradition. According to Daniel Putman, courage involves deliberate choice in the face of fear for a worthy goal, and it depends on an appropriate balance of fear and confidence. Courage does not require the absence of fear.

Idealized, heroic image of a leader, often built through flattery, [[Propaganda|propaganda]], and manipulation of [[Mass media|mass media]]. Techniques include staged spectacles, the arts, government-organized rallies, and the instilling of patriotism. The term is similar to apotheosis, but it relies on modern social engineering and is usually established by the state or ruling party in one-party states. Some of the best-known examples, from the 20th century, surround [[Joseph Stalin]], [[Mao Zedong]], and [[Adolf Hitler]]. The first known political use of the phrase appeared in a letter from [[Karl Marx]] dated November 10, 1877. Such cults are also found in some monarchies and liberal democracies.

Northern constellation on the plane of the [[Milky Way]], named for the Latinized Greek word for swan. It features the Northern Cross asterism and was among the 48 constellations listed by [[Ptolemy]]; it remains one of the 88 modern constellations. Its brightest star, [[Deneb]], marks the tail of the swan and forms one corner of the Summer Triangle. [[Cygnus X-1]], a distant X-ray binary, was the first object widely held to be a [[Black hole|black hole]].

City in central Poland, capital of [[Łódź Voivodeship]] (pop., 2025: 639,890). Located 120 km south-west of [[Warsaw]], it received town rights in 1423 and was long a small settlement in woodland and marsh. Textile manufacturing expanded rapidly from 1850, drawing migrants, many of them Jews and Germans, and the city became multinational. Its architecture contrasted luxurious mansions with red-brick factories and dilapidated tenements. During [[World War II]], German occupiers forced its large Jewish population into the Litzmannstadt Ghetto before deportation to camps. The city is home to the National Film School, which trained [[Andrzej Wajda]], and in 2017 it was named a [[UNESCO]] City of Film.

Second king of the united Kingdom of Israel and leader of the tribe of Judah, according to the [[Hebrew Bible]]. Most knowledge of David comes from biblical literature, whose historicity has been extensively challenged, and his reign may have occurred around the 9th century BC. In the biblical account, he is a shepherd and harpist who kills the Philistine [[Goliath]], then becomes king of Judah and later of all Israel. He conquers [[Jerusalem]] and makes it the capital. The narrative also records his adultery with Bathsheba and the death of her husband, Uriah. Many [[Psalms]] are attributed to him, and the [[Quran]] describes him as an Israelite king and a prophet of God.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series written by Tsugumi Ohba and illustrated by Takeshi Obata. Serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Jump* from December 2003 to May 2006, it follows Light Yagami, a high school student who discovers a notebook that kills anyone whose name is written in it. A 37-episode [[Anime|anime]] adaptation was broadcast in 2006–07, and an American film was released on [[Netflix]] in 2017. By April 2015, the manga had over 30 million copies in circulation, making it one of the best-selling manga series.

Electrical insulator polarized by an applied [[Electric field|electric field]]. Unlike an [[Electrical conductor|electrical conductor]], a dielectric has no loosely bound electrons to carry current. Instead, its charges shift slightly from their average positions, creating an internal field that partly opposes the applied field. The extent to which a material polarizes is expressed by its relative [[Permittivity|permittivity]]. A common example is the insulating material between the plates of a [[Capacitor|capacitor]], where polarization increases the surface charge for a given field strength. The term was coined by [[William Whewell]] at the request of [[Michael Faraday]]. Dielectric properties govern the storage and dissipation of electric and magnetic energy, which matters in electronics, optics, and solid-state physics.

Country in the [[Horn of Africa]] (pop., 2024: 1,066,809). Bordered by Somalia, Ethiopia, and Eritrea, it lies on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, near some of the world's busiest shipping lanes, and controls access to the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. It is the principal maritime port for imports to and exports from neighboring [[Ethiopia]]. Known as French Somaliland from 1897 to 1967, Djibouti voted for independence in 1977 and joined the [[United Nations]] in its first year. French and Arabic are official languages, and about 94% of the population is Muslim. The country hosts foreign military bases, and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development is headquartered in [[Djibouti City]].

Informal group of feces-feeding beetles, mostly in the superfamily Scarabaeoidea. Dung beetles do not form a single [[Clade|clade]], and dung feeding is found in several beetle families. The subfamily Scarabaeinae alone comprises more than 5,000 species. They live on every continent except [[Antarctica]], and most use smell to find dung. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] revered the dung-rolling beetle as the god Khepri, who rolled the sun across the sky. Functional types include rollers, which form and bury dung balls, tunnelers, which bury dung where they find it, and dwellers, which live within dung. By burying dung, the beetles enhance soil fertility and help reduce [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions from dung pats.
